title: How does `satisfies` validate shape without widening literal types?
description: Deep dive into the `satisfies` operator: why it preserves literal inference unlike `as` or annotation, and when to use it for config objects.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="220" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="130" y="85" text-anchor="middle">value { a: 1 }</text><text class="d-sub" x="130" y="105" text-anchor="middle">inferred literal</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="240" y1="90" x2="320" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="320,90 310,84 310,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="330" y="40" width="180" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="420" y="80" text-anchor="middle">satisfies T</text><text class="d-sub" x="420" y="100" text-anchor="middle">validate shape</text><text class="d-sub" x="420" y="115" text-anchor="middle">keep literal</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Type narrowed</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">no widening to T</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** `satisfies` checks assignability to a type while keeping the value's most specific inferred type — unlike `:` or `as`, it never widens.

**Core concept.** `satisfies T` asserts the expression is assignable to `T` but the resulting type stays the **narrowest inferred literal**, so keys, `as const` tuples and discriminants remain precise while still catching excess-property mistakes.

How it works — `const cfg = { mode: "dark", retry: 3 } satisfies Config` validates against `Config` at the declaration site. If `Config` expects `mode: string`, it passes, but `cfg.mode` stays `"dark"` not `string`. With `as Config` or `const cfg: Config = …`, the type widens to `Config` and literal info is lost, so downstream `cfg.mode === "dark"` narrowing breaks. Errors appear at the `satisfies` keyword, not at a distant usage. Chaining `as const satisfies T` works too, but `satisfies` already preserves readonly literals for object literals.

This powers palette / route maps, i18n dictionaries, and theme tokens: you get autocomplete for valid keys and an error if you typo a value, without extracting a separate `typeof cfg` type.

| Syntax | Checks | Result type | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `const x: T = v` | yes | `T` (widened) | exporting public API |
| `v as T` | no (assert) | `T` (forced) | escape hatch, DOM |
| `v satisfies T` | yes | `typeof v` narrowed | config, maps, registry |
| `v as const satisfies T` | yes | `readonly` literals | frozen constants |

> **Tip:** Use `satisfies` for internal config objects where you want both validation and preserved literals; use a type annotation when you intentionally want to widen to the public contract.

```ts
type Theme = { mode: 'light' | 'dark'; scale: number };
const cfg = {
  mode: 'dark',
  scale: 1,
  // @ts-expect-error - typo caught at satisfies, not later
  // extra: true
} satisfies Theme;

// cfg.mode is "dark", not string — narrowing works
if (cfg.mode === 'dark') {
  console.log('dark mode');
}

// vs widening
const cfg2: Theme = { mode: 'dark', scale: 1 };
// cfg2.mode is string — literal lost
type Mode = typeof cfg.mode; // "dark"
type Mode2 = typeof cfg2.mode; // string
```

title: How does `using` / `await using` with `Symbol.dispose` work in TypeScript 5.2+?
description: Explicit Resource Management: `using` declarations, `Disposable` interfaces, scoped LIFO disposal, and how TypeScript types `Symbol.dispose` and `Symbol.asyncDispose`.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">using res =</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">acquire()</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Scope body</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">use res</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">[Symbol.dispose]</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">LIFO on exit</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** `using` declares a block-scoped disposable whose `[Symbol.dispose]()` is called automatically on exit; `await using` does the same for async disposal.

**Core concept.** TypeScript 5.2 types the TC39 Explicit Resource Management proposal: any object with `[Symbol.dispose]: () => void` (or `[Symbol.asyncDispose]: () => Promise<void>`) can be bound with `using` / `await using`. The engine guarantees LIFO disposal even on `throw`/`return` — typed as `Disposable` / `AsyncDisposable`.

How it works — `using file = open()` desugars to `try { … } finally { file[Symbol.dispose]() }` per declaration, in reverse declaration order. TypeScript enforces that `file` is `Disposable` and that `await using` appears only in `async` scopes where dispose returns a `Promise`. `Symbol.dispose` and `Symbol.asyncDispose` are now in `lib.esnext.disposable`. You implement them on classes, and `using` checks assignability. `DisposableStack` / `AsyncDisposableStack` let you compose multiple resources without nesting.

Upgrade: set `target: "es2022"` or higher and `lib: ["esnext.disposable"]`, and enable `esModuleInterop` for polyfilled runtimes; in Node 20+/Bun you get native dispose, elsewhere you need the `explicit-resource-management` polyfill but types still help.

| Declaration | Interface | Dispose timing | Order |
|---|---|---|---|
| `using x = …` | `Disposable` (`[Symbol.dispose]`) | sync on scope exit | LIFO |
| `await using x = …` | `AsyncDisposable` | `await` on exit | LIFO |
| `DisposableStack` | stacks many | `defer()` + `dispose()` | LIFO |
| manual `try/finally` | any | manual | error-prone |

> **Tip:** Prefer `using` over `try/finally` for locks, file handles, and test fixtures; if dispose is async (DB, fetch stream), you must use `await using` or the promise is ignored.

```ts
// lib: esnext.disposable
class TempFile implements Disposable {
  constructor(private path: string) {}
  [Symbol.dispose]() {
    console.log('cleanup', this.path);
  }
}
function work() {
  using f1 = new TempFile('/tmp/a');
  using f2 = new TempFile('/tmp/b');
  console.log('do work');
  // on exit: f2[Symbol.dispose](), then f1 — LIFO
}

// async resource
class Conn implements AsyncDisposable {
  async [Symbol.asyncDispose]() { await this.close(); }
  async close() {}
}
async function fetchScoped() {
  await using c = new Conn();
  await c.close(); // auto disposed even if throw
}

// composing
function batch() {
  using stack = new DisposableStack();
  const a = stack.use(new TempFile('a'));
  const b = stack.use(new TempFile('b'));
  // stack disposed at end — both cleaned
}
```

title: How do TypeScript 5.0 Stage 3 decorators differ from legacy `experimentalDecorators`?
description: Compare new ECMAScript Stage 3 decorators `(value, context)` with old `experimentalDecorators`: signature, order, metadata, and migration pitfalls.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="80" text-anchor="middle">@decorator</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="100" text-anchor="middle">legacy 3 args</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="115" text-anchor="middle">prototype mutate</text><line class="d-edge" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="80" text-anchor="middle">TS 5.0 Stage 3</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="100" text-anchor="middle">(value, context)</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="115" text-anchor="middle">metadata + init</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Clean wrap</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">no descriptor hack</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** TS 5.0 implements Stage 3 decorators as `function(value, context)` with `context.kind`/`metadata`; legacy `experimentalDecorators` used `(target, key, descriptor)` and mutates prototypes — they are incompatible.

**Core concept.** Stage 3 (standard) decorators are pure wrappers called at class-definition time: `function dec(value, context) { return newValue }` where `context` carries `kind: "class"|"method"|"getter"|"field"|"accessor"`, `name`, `metadata`, and `addInitializer`. No descriptor mutation; you return a replacement.

How it works — Legacy TS (`"experimentalDecorators": true`) executed decorators bottom-up with three args and let you mutate `descriptor.value`. Stage 3 is also bottom-up for evaluation but applied top-down wrapping, supports `accessor` (auto-replaces getter+setter pair), `context.metadata` (per-class Symbol.metadata), and `context.addInitializer` to inject per-instance logic (e.g. register). You enable it with no flag in TS 5.0+; to keep legacy you must keep `experimentalDecorators`. Mixing both in one project is a common `TS1238` error — choose one per tsconfig. Tooling (Babel, SWC) must also target stage 3.

Migration cost: `reflect-metadata` and many legacy decorator libraries (TypeORM, Angular <17, MobX) required rewrites or compat shims; new libs use `Symbol.metadata` polyfill.

| Feature | Legacy (experimental) | Stage 3 (TS 5.0+) |
|---|---|---|
| Signature | `(target, key, desc)` | `(value, context)` |
| Kinds | class/method/prop/param | class/method/field/accessor/getter/setter |
| Return | mutate descriptor | return replacement |
| Metadata | `reflect-metadata` | `context.metadata` / `Symbol.metadata` |
| Field | runs on prototype | runs per instance via initializer |

> **Tip:** If you maintain a library, ship both builds or document required `experimentalDecorators: false`; use `context.addInitializer` instead of constructor patching for per-instance state.

```ts
// Stage 3 — TS 5.0+
function logged(value: any, context: ClassDecoratorContext) {
  console.log('define', context.name);
  return value;
}
function bound<This, Args extends any[], R>(
  fn: (this: This, ...a: Args) => R,
  ctx: ClassMethodDecoratorContext<This, (this: This, ...a: Args) => R>
) {
  ctx.addInitializer(function (this: This) {
    // per-instance bind example handled via return wrapper
  });
  return function (this: This, ...a: Args) {
    return fn.apply(this, a);
  };
}

@logged
class Store {
  @bound
  get() { return 42; }
}

// legacy — different runtime
// @sealed
// class Old { @readonly prop = 1 } // needs experimentalDecorators
```

title: What are `const` type parameters (`<const T>`) and why are they better than `as const`?
description: TypeScript 5.0 `const` generics: how `<const T>` infers readonly literal/tuple types automatically and where it beats `as const` assertions.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="220" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="130" y="85" text-anchor="middle">fn<T>(arr: T[])</text><text class="d-sub" x="130" y="105" text-anchor="middle">T widens</text><line class="d-edge" x1="240" y1="90" x2="320" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="320,90 310,84 310,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="330" y="40" width="180" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="420" y="85" text-anchor="middle"><const T></text><text class="d-sub" x="420" y="105" text-anchor="middle">keep readonly literal</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">["a","b"]</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">readonly ["a","b"]</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** `<const T>` tells the compiler to infer `T` as if the argument were written `as const` — producing `readonly` literal unions/tuples without a call-site assertion.

**Core concept.** Without `const`, `function f<T>(x: T)` widens `"a"` to `string` and `[1,2]` to `number[]`. Writing `function f<const T>(x: T)` opts that parameter into const-context inference: literals stay literals, arrays become `readonly` tuples, objects become `readonly` with literal props.

How it works — At inference, the `const` modifier changes the inference priority: `inferFriend<const T>(["a","b"])` yields `readonly ["a","b"]` not `string[]`, so you can derive `T[number]` as `"a" | "b"`. This is viral only for that param — other params still widen normally. It replaces call-site `as const` hacks and the overload dance `function foo<T extends string>(x: T[])` vs `readonly T[]`. Constraint still respects `extends`, and you can combine `<const T extends string>` to keep string-only narrowing.

Trade-off: `const T` makes `T` `readonly` deeply, so mutating methods (`push`) disappear — intentional for immutable APIs. For mutable copies, use `NoInfer` or copy via `[...t]`.

| Call | `<T>` (no const) | `<const T>` | Use case |
|---|---|---|---|
| `f(["a","b"])` | `string[]` | `readonly ["a","b"]` | tuple routes |
| `f({x:1})` | `{x:number}` | `{readonly x:1}` | config literals |
| `f("hi")` | `string` | `"hi"` | branded literals |
| `g<const T>(t:T)` + mutate | allow | error (readonly) | immutable API |

> **Tip:** Use `<const T>` on factory helpers (`createRoute`, `defineConfig`) so callers never need `as const`; don't use it if you intend to mutate the inferred value inside the function.

```ts
function defineRoutes<const T extends readonly string[]>(routes: T): T {
  return routes;
}
const r = defineRoutes(['/home', '/about']);
// r is readonly ["/home","/about"] — no as const needed
type Route = typeof r[number]; // "/home" | "/about"

function get<const T>(x: T): T { return x; }
const a = get(['a','b']); // readonly ["a","b"]
const b = get({ x: 1 as const }); // still {readonly x: 1}

// Without const — widened
function get2<T>(x: T): T { return x; }
const c = get2(['a','b']); // string[]
```

title: Why are conditional types distributive and how do you control it with `infer`?
description: Explain distributive conditional types, naked type params, `infer` extraction, and wrapping in `[]` to suppress distribution.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">T extends U ?</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">naked T</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Distributes</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">A|B => (A ?)(B ?)</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">[T] wraps</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">no distribute</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** Conditionals on a naked `T` distribute over unions (`T extends U ? X : Y` maps each member); wrap `T` in `[]` or use `infer` to suppress or extract.

**Core concept.** `type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never` is distributive: `ToArray<string|number>` -> `string[] | number[]`, not `(string|number)[]`. This enables `infer` extractions like `type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T` to work per-union member.

How it works — Distribution triggers only when the checked type is a **naked type param** (`T` directly). Using `[T] extends [U] ? …` or `T extends any ? …` inside a tuple disables it. `infer` introduces a fresh variable to capture — e.g. `type Return<T> = T extends (...a:any)=> infer R ? R : never`. For deep patterns, combine: `type Deep<T> = T extends (infer E)[] ? Deep<E> : T`. To keep unions intact, wrap: `type NoDist<T> = [T] extends [string] ? true : false` -> `NoDist<string|number>` is `false`, not `boolean`.

Pitfall: excessive distributive recursion hits the 50-level instantiation limit — add tail-recursion or `NoInfer` guards.

| Pattern | Distributes? | Result on `A|B` | Tip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `T extends U ? X : Y` (naked) | yes | `(A?X:Y) | (B?X:Y)` | default |
| `[T] extends [U] ? X : Y` | no | single check | suppress |
| `T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : never` | yes | per-member unwrap | extract |
| `T extends any ? T[] : never` | yes | `A[]|B[]` | map unions |

> **Tip:** `infer` never appears alone — always inside `extends`; to stop distribution when extracting from a union-wrapped promise, use `[T] extends [Promise<infer V>]` intentionally.

```ts
type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never;
type A = ToArray<string | number>; // string[] | number[]

type NonDist<T> = [T] extends [string] ? true : false;
type B = NonDist<string | number>; // false (not boolean)

type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T;
type C = Unwrap<Promise<string> | Promise<number>>; // string | number

type Return<T> = T extends (...a: any) => infer R ? R : never;
type R = Return<() => string>; // string

// extract array element deeply
type Elem<T> = T extends (infer E)[] ? E : T;
type E = Elem<string[] | number[]>; // string | number
```

title: What does `NoInfer<T>` do and when should you block inference?
description: TypeScript 5.4's `NoInfer<T>`: lower-priority inference, API design where you want one param to win over another.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">infer site</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">fn<T>(x: T)</text><line class="d-edge" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">NoInfer<T></text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">block inference</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Use default T</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">not widened site</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** `NoInfer<T>` marks a position as non-inferential so the compiler doesn't use that argument to infer `T`; it only checks assignability after `T` is fixed from other sites.

**Core concept.** Before 5.4, every occurrence of `T` competed equally during inference. If a function had `create(a: T, b: NoInfer<T>)`, `b` could incorrectly widen `T`. `NoInfer<T>` (implemented as `T & {}`-like intrinsic) lowers that site's inference priority to zero.

How it works — `function eq<T>(a: T, b: NoInfer<T>)` infers `T` solely from `a`; `b` is then checked against that `T`. This fixes `declare function useState<T>(initial: T, setter: NoInfer<T>):` scenarios and `createAction<T>({ type: string, payload: NoInfer<T> })`. Prior hacks used `T & {}` or `T & unknown` but leaked into errors and tooltips; `NoInfer` is opaque and documented. It also interacts with `const` params — `foo<const T>(x: T, y: NoInfer<T>)` still keeps `x` literal-narrowed.

When to use: builder APIs where one argument is canonical (schema, default value) and the other must conform without influencing inference.

| API | Without `NoInfer` | With `NoInfer` | Winner |
|---|---|---|---|
| `equal(a: T, b: T)` | `equal("a","b")` infers `T="a"|"b"` (wide) | `equal<T>(a:T,b:NoInfer<T>)` | `T` from `a` only |
| `create(opts: T, cb: (x:T)=>void)` | `cb` widens `T` | `cb: (x:NoInfer<T>)=>void` | `opts` wins |
| `define<const T>(x:T, y:T)` | both compete | `y:NoInfer<T>` | `x` literal wins |

> **Tip:** Use `NoInfer` sparingly — adding it everywhere hides useful inference. Prefer `satisfies` when you want validation without widening at the declaration site.

```ts
// TS 5.4+
declare function equals<const T>(a: T, b: NoInfer<T>): boolean;
equals('a', 'a'); // ok
// @ts-expect-error — 'b' must be 'a', not string
equals('a', 'b');

type Action<T> = { type: string; payload: NoInfer<T> };
declare function create<T>(p: T): Action<T>;
// T inferred only from arg, payload checked
const a = create({ id: 1 }); // T = {id:number}

// hand-rolled before 5.4 (leaky)
type OldNoInfer<T> = T & {};
```

title: When should you use `moduleResolution: "bundler"` versus `"nodenext"`?
description: Compare bundler vs nodenext/node16: how imports are resolved, file extensions, `allowImportingTsExtensions`, and when each breaks.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">import "x"</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">.ts / .js?</text><line class="d-edge" x1="220" y1="65" x2="300" y2="65"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,65 290,59 290,71"/><rect class="d-box" x="310" y="10" width="190" height="70" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="405" y="40" text-anchor="middle">bundler</text><text class="d-sub" x="405" y="58" text-anchor="middle">no check, trust bundler</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="115" x2="300" y2="115"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,115 290,109 290,121"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="95" width="190" height="70" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="405" y="125" text-anchor="middle">nodenext</text><text class="d-sub" x="405" y="143" text-anchor="middle">strict ESM/CJS</text><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Resolution</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">.d.ts vs emit</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** `bundler` trusts the bundler (Vite/esbuild) and skips extension checks; `nodenext` enforces Node ESM/CJS reality — you must write the runtime-correct specifier.

**Core concept.** `moduleResolution: "bundler"` (TS 5.0+) is for Vite/Next/esbuild/Webpack: you can `import {x} from "./x"` without extension, bare specifiers map to `node_modules`, and types resolve loosely. `moduleResolution: "nodenext"` is for Node native ESM/CJS dual packages: you must write the **emitted** specifier — usually `"./x.js"` even from `.ts`, and `package.json` `"exports"`/`"type":"module"` matter.

How it works — Under `bundler`, TS never checks that `"./x"` maps to `"./x.ts"` vs `"./x.js"` at runtime; the bundler does. With `allowImportingTsExtensions`, you may even `import "./x.ts"` (erased at emit). Under `nodenext`, TS enforces Node's algorithm: `.js` required from `.ts` ESM, `.ts` imports error, and `exports` conditions pick types (`types` condition). Mismatched `type: module` + CJS `require` yields `TS1471`. Vite + `nodenext` breaks on extensionless relative imports; Node + `bundler` hides runtime `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`.

Choice: apps with bundler -> `bundler`; libraries/Node CLIs -> `nodenext` plus `verbatimModuleSyntax` and `.js` extensions.

| Setting | Allows `./a`? | Requires `.js`? | Checks `exports`? | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `bundler` | yes | no | loosely | Vite/Next/Webpack apps |
| `nodenext` | no (must `.js`) | yes | strictly | Node libraries, dual pkg |
| `node16` | similar to nodenext | yes | yes | legacy Node |
| `bundler` + `allowImportingTsExtensions` | `import "./a.ts"` | N/A | — | single-file emit |

> **Tip:** For libraries, set `"module": "nodenext"`, `"moduleResolution": "nodenext"`, write `import "./foo.js"` from `.ts`; enable `attw` to catch drift.

```ts
// tsconfig for Vite app
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "esnext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true
  }
}

// tsconfig for Node library
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "nodenext",
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
    "target": "es2022",
    "declaration": true
  }
}

// ESM source must use .js extension under nodenext
import { foo } from './foo.js'; // ok even though file is foo.ts
import { bar } from './bar'; // error under nodenext
```

title: What does `arethetypeswrong` (attw) detect and how do you fix false ESM/CJS packages?
description: Using `arethetypeswrong` / `attw` to audit dual packages: `FalseESM`, `FalseCJS`, `CJSResolvesToESM`, missing `types` condition, and the correct `exports` map.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">dual pkg</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">CJS + ESM</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="220" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="420" y="85" text-anchor="middle">arethetypeswrong</text><text class="d-sub" x="420" y="105" text-anchor="middle">attw --pack</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="530" y1="90" x2="610" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="610,90 600,84 600,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="620" y="40" width="180" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="710" y="85" text-anchor="middle">false ESM?</text><text class="d-sub" x="710" y="105" text-anchor="middle">.js vs .d.ts mismatch</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** `arethetypeswrong` (github.com/arethetypeswrong/arethetypeswrong) simulates every consumer resolver (ESM, CJS, bundler) and flags when resolved types don't match runtime JS.

**Core concept.** `npx @arethetypeswrong/cli --pack` packs your built package and resolution-tests each `exports` entry via `cjs`, `esm`, `bundler` conditions. It reports `FalseCJS` (CJS import hits ESM types), `FalseESM` (ESM hits CJS), `Missing`/`Unexpected` files, and `CJSResolvesToESM` canary patterns.

How it works — TS types are separate from JS: `exports: { ".": { "import": "./dist/index.js", "require": "./dist/index.cjs" } }` needs mirrored `types`/`default` or `types` conditions: `"import": { "types": "./dist/index.d.mts", "default": "./dist/index.js" }`. Single `types: "./dist/index.d.ts"` with only a CJS `.js` is classified `FalseESM` and causes `TS1472`. `attw` also checks `type: module` + `.js` is ESM vs `commonjs` package and warns on extension mismatch. Fix: dual emit (`tsc` twice or `tsup`), set `"types"` per condition, and add `"exports"` not just `"main"`/`"types"`.

Run `attw` in CI; unlike `tsc --checkJs`, it catches package boundary errors only consumers see.

| attw diagnostic | Meaning | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `FalseESM` | ESM import got CJS types | emit `.d.mts` + `types` under `import` |
| `FalseCJS` | CJS `require` got ESM types | emit `.d.cts` + `types` under `require` |
| `CJSResolvesToESM` | CJS fallback is ESM JS | add real `.cjs` boundary |
| `Missing types` | `exports` has no `types` | add `types` condition first |

> **Tip:** Emit types per format (`index.d.ts`/`d.mts`/`d.cts`) and order `types` first in each condition — bundlers pick the first match.

```ts
// package.json - correct dual package
{
  "name": "lib",
  "type": "commonjs",
  "exports": {
    ".": {
      "import": {
        "types": "./dist/index.d.mts",
        "default": "./dist/index.mjs"
      },
      "require": {
        "types": "./dist/index.d.cts",
        "default": "./dist/index.cjs"
      }
    }
  }
}
// check
// npx @arethetypeswrong/cli --pack
// npx tsc --traceResolution to debug
```

title: What does `verbatimModuleSyntax` enforce and why did it replace `importsNotUsedAsValues`?
description: The TS 5.0 `verbatimModuleSyntax` flag: required `import type` / `export type`, `allowSyntheticDefaultImports` interactions, and migration from `importsNotUsedAsValues: remove`.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="230" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="135" y="85" text-anchor="middle">import { type T }</text><text class="d-sub" x="135" y="105" text-anchor="middle">erased at emit</text><line class="d-edge" x1="250" y1="90" x2="330" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="330,90 320,84 320,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="340" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="440" y="85" text-anchor="middle">verbatimModuleSyntax</text><text class="d-sub" x="440" y="105" text-anchor="middle">must use type keyword</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="540" y1="90" x2="620" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="620,90 610,84 610,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="630" y="40" width="170" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="715" y="85" text-anchor="middle">0 runtime bug</text><text class="d-sub" x="715" y="105" text-anchor="middle">no elided value</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` makes type imports syntactic: you must write `import type {T}` and `export type {T}`; the compiler never rewrites or elides imports on semantics alone.

**Core concept.** Before 5.0, TS erased `import { T }` if `T` was only used as a type, based on the checker — fragile when emit was done by Babel/SWC with `isolatedModules`. `verbatimModuleSyntax` removes type analysis from emit: any `import` without `type` is preserved as JS; `import type` is erased entirely. This aligns emit across all tools.

How it works — Enable `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` (replaces `importsNotUsedAsValues` and `preserveValueImports`). Now `import { Foo } from "./foo"` where `Foo` is a type is an error: `TS1484: 'Foo' is a type and must be imported using a type-only import`. Fix with `import type { Foo }` or `import { type Foo, bar } from "./foo"` (inline type). Same for `export`. `allowSyntheticDefaultImports` and `esModuleInterop` still affect shape but not erasure. `import type` also works with `verbatimModuleSyntax` off, but the flag forces consistency.

CJS interop: `import type` never produces `require()` in output; `import { type T, value }` emits only `value`.

| Import | `verbatimModuleSyntax: false` | `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` | Emit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `import { T }` (type-only) | erased if unused as value | error, need `import type` | none |
| `import type { T }` | erased | erased | none |
| `import { type T, v }` | `v` only | `v` only | `import {v}` |
| `export type { T }` | erased | erased | none |

> **Tip:** Codemod with `npx typescript-codemod` or `eslint --fix` (`@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports`); inline `import { type T }` keeps one line per module.

```ts
// tsconfig: { "verbatimModuleSyntax": true, "isolatedModules": true }
import type { Props } from './props'; // erased
import { type Config, createConfig } from './config'; // only createConfig emitted
import { value } from './value'; // preserved even if only used as type elsewhere -> error to fix

type Local = Props & { extra: string };
export type { Local }; // must be type export
export { createConfig }; // value export preserved

// wrong under verbatimModuleSyntax
// import { Props } from './props'; // TS1484
```

title: What is `isolatedDeclarations` and how does it enable single-file transpilation for declaration emit?
description: TypeScript 5.5 `isolatedDeclarations`: generating `.d.ts` without whole-program analysis for tools like `oxc`, `swc`, `esbuild` + `tsgo`.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">TS file</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">code + types</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="220" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="420" y="85" text-anchor="middle">isolatedDeclarations</text><text class="d-sub" x="420" y="105" text-anchor="middle">emit .d.ts alone</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="530" y1="90" x2="610" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="610,90 600,84 600,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="620" y="40" width="180" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="710" y="85" text-anchor="middle">No checker needed</text><text class="d-sub" x="710" y="105" text-anchor="middle">oxc / swc / esbuild</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** `isolatedDeclarations: true` requires each file's types to be inferrable from that file alone so `.d.ts` can be emitted in parallel without cross-file type checking.

**Core concept.** Traditional `declaration: true` needs the full checker — slow and incompatible with isolated transpilers (`oxc`, `swc`, `esbuild`). `isolatedDeclarations` enforces that every exported declaration has an explicit resolvable type from its file, so tools can emit `.d.ts` per file in isolation, like Babel but for types. Introduced in TS 5.5 and required for `tsgo` and `unplugin-isolated-decl`.

How it works — With `isolatedDeclarations: true`, `export const x = cond ? "a" : 1` errors: `TS9010: variable must have explicit type`. Add `: string | number`. Similarly, `export function f(x) { return x }` needs param/return annotation because `x` type can't be inferred from other files. Computed, `satisfies`, and re-exports via `export * from "…"` are restricted — they leak cross-file inference. `verbatimModuleSyntax` plus this flag ensures type-only imports don't affect declaration emit. Runtime `tsc` with `--isolatedDeclarations` + `esbuild` can now produce JS + `.d.ts` in parallel at build speed.

Whitelisting: add explicit `any` to opt out locally.

| Code | Without `isolatedDeclarations` | With `isolatedDeclarations: true` | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `export const x = get()` | infers from `get()` | error — needs `: T` | add return type to `get` + annotation |
| `export function f(x){}` | inferred `any` | error — param needs type | `f(x: string)` |
| `export const y = obj as const satisfies T` | ok | error — cross-file | annotate `y: T` |
| `export type T = infer…` | computed | error if needs checker | annotate |

> **Tip:** Turn it on in libraries early; add `publint` + `attw` to verify dual emit and use `unplugin-isolated-decl` (oxc) or `tsdown` for parallel builds.

```ts
// tsconfig: { "declaration": true, "isolatedDeclarations": true, "verbatimModuleSyntax": true }
import type { User } from './user';

// bad — needs annotation
// export const getUser = (id) => fetchUser(id);
// export const x = Math.random() > 0.5 ? "a" : 1;

// good explicit
export const getUser = (id: string): Promise<User> => fetchUser(id);
export const x: string | number = Math.random() > 0.5 ? "a" : 1;

export function format(u: User): string { return u.name; }

// re-export needs types available
export type { User };
declare function fetchUser(id: string): Promise<User>;
```

title: How does TypeScript 5.5 infer type predicates for `Array.filter` automatically?
description: TS 5.5 inferred type predicates: `filter` no longer needs manual `is T` annotations when callback returns a truthiness check.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">arr.filter(x=>!!x)</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">predicate?</text><line class="d-edge" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle"><TS 5.5</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">still (T | falsy)[]</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">5.5 infer predicate</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">T narrowed auto</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** TS 5.5 control-flow analyzes `array.filter(x => x !== undefined)` and, when the callback's `if` refines `T`, infers the result as the narrowed type — e.g. `(string|undefined)[]` -> `string[]`.

**Core concept.** Previously `arr.filter(Boolean)` or `x => typeof x === "string"` kept `string|undefined` unless you wrote `filter((x): x is string => …)`. In 5.5+, the compiler treats arrow/filter callbacks as predicate positions and lifts control-flow narrowing into the return type, synthesizing `is` predicates for you.

How it works — If the callback's last expression is a type guard (`x != null`, `typeof x === "string"`, `x in obj`, `!!x` with `strictNullChecks`), the checker propagates the narrowed type to `filter`'s result. This works for `Array.filter`, `find`, `every`, `some`, and user receivers annotated with predicate positions. It does *not* infer for complex indirect calls (`const f = x=> !!x; arr.filter(f)`) — inline only. To opt out, annotate the callback return as `boolean`; to force, annotate as `is T`.

Also enables faster narrowing for `using`? No — separate feature. This relies on `lib.es5.d.ts` change where `filter` is now declared with `predicate: (value: T, …) => value is S` overloads.

| Callback | TS 5.4 result | TS 5.5 inferred | Need manual `is`? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `filter(x => x != null)` | `(T| null)[]` | `T[]` | no |
| `filter(x => typeof x === "string")` | still `string|number[]`? | `string[]` | no |
| `filter(Boolean)` | `T[]` | `NonNullable<T>[]` | no (builtin overload) |
| `const g = x=>!!x; filter(g)` | `T[]` | `T[]` (no infer) | yes — inline or annotate |

> **Tip:** Inline the predicate for inference; extract to a named `isNonNull` helper with explicit `x is T` if you reuse it across files.

```ts
const arr: (string | undefined)[] = ['a', undefined, 'b'];
// TS 5.5: inferred as string[]
const clean = arr.filter(x => x !== undefined);
clean satisfies string[]; // ok

const mixed: (string | number)[] = [1, 'a', 2];
const strings = mixed.filter(x => typeof x === 'string');
// strings: string[]

const byBool = arr.filter(Boolean); // (string | undefined)[] -> string[]
// before 5.5 you wrote:
// const clean2 = arr.filter((x): x is string => x !== undefined);

// not inferred — out of line
const isTruthy = (x: unknown) => !!x;
const stillWide = arr.filter(isTruthy); // still (string|undefined)[]
```

title: What's new to type in TypeScript 5.5+ libs — `Array.fromAsync`, `Set` methods, `Iterator` helpers?
description: New built-in lib types in TS 5.5/5.6/5.8: `Array.fromAsync`, `Iterator` helpers, `Set` algebra, `Map.groupBy`/`Object.groupBy`, `Error.isError`, regex `v` flag.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box-accent" x="20" y="40" width="220" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="130" y="85" text-anchor="middle">TS 5.5+ libs</text><text class="d-sub" x="130" y="105" text-anchor="middle">5.5 / 5.6 / 5.8</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="240" y1="90" x2="320" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="320,90 310,84 310,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="330" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="430" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Iterator / Set</text><text class="d-sub" x="430" y="105" text-anchor="middle">Array.fromAsync</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="530" y1="90" x2="610" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="610,90 600,84 600,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="620" y="40" width="180" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="710" y="85" text-anchor="middle">lib: esnext</text><text class="d-sub" x="710" y="105" text-anchor="middle">typed helpers</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** TS 5.5+ ships `lib.esnext` updates: `Array.fromAsync`, `Set.prototype.union/intersection/difference/symmetricDifference/isSubsetOf/isSupersetOf/isDisjointFrom`, `Iterator.from` helpers, `Object/Map.groupBy`, and strict `Error.isError` / `Promise.withResolvers`.

**Core concept.** Each ECMAScript addition lands with types under `lib` targets. TS 5.6 added `Iterator.prototype` helpers (`map`, `filter`, `take`, `flatMap`, `toArray`) as `Iterator<T>`; 5.5 added `Set` algebra methods; 5.6/5.7 added `Array.fromAsync`; 5.8 typed `Error.isError`, `Promise.try`. You get them by setting `target`/`lib` to `esnext` or `es2024`.

How it works — With `"lib": ["esnext"]` (or `"es2024"` + `"esnext.collection"`/`"esnext.iterator"`), `arr.values().filter(x=> x>1).take(2).toArray()` is typed as `Iterator` chaining without intermediate arrays. `Set` methods are generic over `SetLike`. `Array.fromAsync` is typed to consume `AsyncIterable` and return `Promise<T[]>`. `Object.groupBy`/`Map.groupBy` are typed with overloads preserving key types. Without correct `lib`, you get `Property does not exist`.

Tip: `Iterator` is lazy — unlike `Array`, helpers are not eager; typing preserves laziness via `Iterator<T>`.

| Feature | `lib` needed | Returns | Since |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Array.fromAsync(iter)` | `es2024`/`esnext` | `Promise<T[]>` | TS 5.7 |
| `Iterator.from(x).map(f).toArray()` | `esnext.iterator` | `Iterator<U>` -> `U[]` | TS 5.6 |
| `Set#union/intersection` | `esnext.collection` | `Set<T>` | TS 5.6 |
| `Object.groupBy` / `Map.groupBy` | `esnext.collection` | `Record<K,T[]> / Map<K,T[]>` | TS 5.6 |
| `Error.isError(e)` | `esnext.error` | `e is Error` | TS 5.8 |

> **Tip:** Set `lib: ["es2022","esnext.disposable","esnext.collection","dom"]` explicitly if you target older `target` but need new types — `esnext` includes all.

```ts
// tsconfig: { "target": "es2022", "lib": ["es2022", "esnext", "dom"] }

async function demo() {
  const it = Iterator.from([1, 2, 3]).map(x => x * 2).filter(x => x > 2);
  const arr = it.toArray(); // number[] — lazy chain, then materialize

  const s1 = new Set([1,2,3]);
  const s2 = new Set([2,3,4]);
  const u = s1.union(s2); // Set<number> {1,2,3,4}
  const inter = s1.intersection(s2); // Set<number> {2,3}

  const grouped = Object.groupBy(['a','bb','c'], s => s.length);
  // grouped: Partial<Record<number, string[]>>

  const asyncArr = await Array.fromAsync(asyncGen());
  Error.isError(new Error()); // true, typed as (e is Error)

  // regex v flag now typed
  const re = /[\p{Emoji}--\p{ASCII}]/v;
}
async function* asyncGen(){ yield 1; yield 2; }
```

title: How do you type and compose multiple disposables with `DisposableStack` and `AsyncDisposableStack`?
description: Practical `DisposableStack` patterns: `stack.use`, `stack.defer`, `stack.adopt`, `move`, and correctly typing `Symbol.asyncDispose` composition.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">using res =</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">acquire()</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Scope body</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">use res</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">[Symbol.dispose]</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">LIFO on exit</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** `DisposableStack` lets you register many `Disposable | () => void` entries via `use/defer/adopt` and dispose them LIFO with `stack.dispose()` — typed to aggregate sync and async resources.

**Core concept.** `new DisposableStack()` holds a LIFO stack. `stack.use(resource)` adds a `Disposable`, `stack.defer(() => cleanup())` adds a bare function, `stack.adopt(value, dispose)` tracks non-disposable values. `stack.move()` transfers ownership without disposing, avoiding double-dispose.

How it works — TypeScript declares `interface DisposableStack extends Disposable { use<T extends Disposable | null>(v: T): T; defer(fn: () => void): void; adopt<T>(v: T, fn: (v:T)=>void): T; move(): DisposableStack; }` and similarly `AsyncDisposableStack`. `using stack = new DisposableStack()` guarantees `stack[Symbol.dispose]()` at scope exit — all registered items dispose in reverse. Mixing sync and async stacks is illegal: async resources must go in `AsyncDisposableStack` under `await using`. `SuppressedError` aggregates errors if multiple disposes throw.

Pattern: create stack early, `use` each acquire, return `stack.move()` to hand ownership to caller without cleanup.

| Method | Takes | Ownership | Error handling |
|---|---|---|---|
| `use(d)` | `Disposable` | stack owns, returns same | `SuppressedError` chain |
| `defer(fn)` | `() => void` | function | LIFO, aggregates |
| `adopt(v, fn)` | value + disposer | stack owns | fn receives v |
| `move()` | — | caller's stack | prevents dispose on old |

> **Tip:** Use `stack.defer(() => close())` for legacy close functions instead of wrapping in a class; `move()` is how you return a stack from a factory without disposing prematurely.

```ts
// typed composition
function openAll() {
  using stack = new DisposableStack();
  const file = stack.use(openFile('/tmp/a')); // Disposable
  stack.defer(() => console.log('defer log'));
  const conn = stack.adopt({ id: 1 }, v => console.log('adopt', v.id));

  if (Math.random() > 0.5) {
    // hand off ownership — stack no longer disposes file
    return stack.move();
  }
  // on throw/return, file -> adopt -> defer in reverse
  return stack;
}

async function asyncBatch() {
  await using stack = new AsyncDisposableStack();
  stack.use(await openAsyncConn());
  stack.defer(async () => await flush());
  // await dispose at scope end
}

declare function openFile(p: string): Disposable;
declare function openAsyncConn(): Promise<AsyncDisposable>;
declare function flush(): Promise<void>;
```

title: How do you use `infer` to build deep `Awaited`, `ReturnType` and `Unwrap` utilities?
description: Hands-on `infer` patterns: extracting promise values, function returns, array elements, and recursively unwrapping nested types without hitting recursion limits.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">T extends U ?</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">naked T</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Distributes</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">A|B => (A ?)(B ?)</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">[T] wraps</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">no distribute</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** `infer R` captures a type inside `extends` so you can name and reuse it — `T extends Promise<infer R> ? R : T` unwraps one layer; recursion handles arbitrary depth.

**Core concept.** `infer` only appears in conditional true-branch: `T extends Foo<infer X> ? X : never` extracts `X`. Combine distribution and recursion to peel layers: built-in `Awaited<T>` recursively awaits promises; `ReturnType<T>` extracts via `(...args:any)=> infer R`.

How it works — `type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? Unwrap<V> : T` handles `Promise<Promise<string>>`. To avoid distributing over unions unintentionally, wrap: `[T] extends [Promise<infer V>] ? …` Distribution is useful when you want per-member extract (`T extends any ? …` maps). Recursion depth is capped (~50 levels) so guard with tail checks. For functions, `infer` can capture args tuple too: `T extends (a: infer A, b: infer B) => any ? [A,B] : never`.

Edge: inferring from overloads picks the last signature; use `T extends { (...a: infer P): any }` carefully.

| Utility | `infer` pattern | Example `T` -> result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Awaited` | `T extends Promise<infer V> ? Awaited<V> : T` | `Promise<Promise<number>>` -> `number` |
| `ReturnType` | `T extends (...a:any)=> infer R ? R : never` | `()=>string` -> `string` |
| `ElementOf` | `T extends (infer E)[] ? E : T` | `string[]` -> `string` |
| `SecondArg` | `T extends (a:any,b: infer B)=>any ? B : never` | `(x,y:number)=>void` -> `number` |

> **Tip:** Prefer built-in `Awaited` over hand-rolled; when writing custom `DeepAwaited`, add a distribution toggle `NoDist<T>` to control union behavior.

```ts
type DeepAwaited<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? DeepAwaited<V> : T;
type A = DeepAwaited<Promise<Promise<string>>>; // string

type Return<T> = T extends (...a: any) => infer R ? R : never;
type R = Return<() => { x: number }>; // {x:number}

type Elem<T> = T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? E : never;
type E = Elem<readonly ['a','b']>; // 'a' | 'b'

// non-distributive unwrap to keep union as group
type UnwrapNonDist<T> = [T] extends [Promise<infer V>] ? V : T;
type B = UnwrapNonDist<Promise<string> | number>; // string

// extract second arg
type Second<T> = T extends (a: any, b: infer B, ...r:any) => any ? B : never;
type S = Second<(x:string, y:number)=>void>; // number
```

title: How does `allowImportingTsExtensions` work with `moduleResolution: "bundler"` and `.ts` imports?
description: When to allow `import "./x.ts"`: interaction with `bundler`, `nodenext`, `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`, `verbatimModuleSyntax`, and emitted `.js` shape.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">import "x"</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">.ts / .js?</text><line class="d-edge" x1="220" y1="65" x2="300" y2="65"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,65 290,59 290,71"/><rect class="d-box" x="310" y="10" width="190" height="70" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="405" y="40" text-anchor="middle">bundler</text><text class="d-sub" x="405" y="58" text-anchor="middle">no check, trust bundler</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="115" x2="300" y2="115"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,115 290,109 290,121"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="95" width="190" height="70" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="405" y="125" text-anchor="middle">nodenext</text><text class="d-sub" x="405" y="143" text-anchor="middle">strict ESM/CJS</text><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Resolution</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">.d.ts vs emit</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** `allowImportingTsExtensions: true` lets you write `import "./x.ts"`; only matters with `bundler`/`nodenext` where TS can erase or rewrite the `.ts` extension at emit.

**Core concept.** Normally you must import `"./x.js"` under `nodenext` and bare `"./x"` under `bundler`. `allowImportingTsExtensions` relaxes the checker to accept `"./x.ts"`, `"./x.mts"`, `"./x.cts"`. Combined with `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` or bundler handling, `.ts` is rewritten to `.js`/`.mjs` at emit so runtime sees JS.

How it works — Flag requires `noEmit` or emit-capable partner that understands rewriting. With `"allowImportingTsExtensions": true` and `"rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true` (TS 5.8+), `import "./a.ts"` emits as `import "./a.js"`. Without rewrite, bundlers like Vite/esbuild resolve `.ts` directly, so no rewrite needed. Under `nodenext`, plain `.ts` imports still need the flag; without it `TS5097` fires. `verbatimModuleSyntax` + `isolatedDeclarations` like explicit extensions because declaration emit can't resolve ambiguous `"./a"`.

When not to use: libraries publishing raw TS should avoid leaking `.ts` imports to consumers — emit should be `.js` only.

| tsconfig combo | Import allowed | Emit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bundler` no flag | `"./a"` / `"./a.js"` | as written (bundler resolves) |
| `bundler` + `allowImportingTsExtensions` | `"./a.ts"` also | preserved (bundler) or rewritten |
| `nodenext` no flag | `"./a.js"` only | `"./a.js"` |
| `nodenext` + flag + `rewrite…` | `"./a.ts"` | `"./a.js"` |
| `isolatedDeclarations` | prefer explicit | needs rewrite |

> **Tip:** In apps use `bundler` with extensionless imports for cleaner diffs; in Node libraries use `nodenext` + `.js` imports and avoid `allowImportingTsExtensions` unless you also enable rewrite and test with `attw`.

```ts
// tsconfig bundler-style
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "esnext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true
  }
}
import { foo } from './foo.ts'; // allowed, emits ./foo.js
import { bar } from './bar.js'; // also allowed

// nodenext ESM must write .js but source is .ts
// foo.ts exists, import is ./foo.js — but with flag you may write ./foo.ts and rewrite
```

title: How do you fix JSX and type-only import errors under `verbatimModuleSyntax`?
description: Common `verbatimModuleSyntax` breaks in React/Next: JSX factory types, `import type` for props, and `export type` pitfalls.
answer: **TL;DR:** Under `verbatimModuleSyntax`, any `import { Props }` used only as a JSX prop type must be `import type { Props }`; otherwise you ship a runtime import that Vercel/Node may tree-shake differently. **Core concept.** React components often `import { User } from "./types"` where `User` is only a type. Before `verbatimModuleSyntax`, TS silently erased it. Now it errors (`TS1484`) and, if you ignore via `// @ts-ignore`, you emit a real `import { User }` that bundles unnecessarily or breaks with `isolatedModules` transpilers that don't know it's a type. How it works — Fix by auditing imports per file: value-used imports stay `import { foo }`; type-only become `import type { Props }` or inline `import { type Props, Component }`. For JSX, `import type { FC } from "react"` plus `import { useState } from "react"` splits cleanly. Re-exports of types need `export type { MyProps }`. `jsx: "react-jsx"` still synthesizes `jsx/jsxs` imports — keep `verbatimModuleSyntax` but ensure `jsxImportSource` types are `type`-only where applicable. Automate: enable `eslint-plugin-import` or `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports` with `fixStyle: inline-type-imports` and run `tsc --noEmit` in CI. | File | Before (erased) | After `verbatimModuleSyntax` | Runtime | |---|---|---|---| | `import { Props }` type-only | erased | error -> `import type { Props}` | no JS | | `import { Comp, type Props }` | half erased (checker) | `Comp` stays, `Props` erased | only `Comp` | | `export { Props }` | erased if type | need `export type { Props }` | no JS | | JSX `import React` | needed for classic | `react-jsx` adds `jsx()` auto | check factory | > **Tip:** Run `npx tsc --noEmit` with `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` and fix all `TS1484` at once; keep React Server Components where value/type split matters for `"use client"` boundaries. ```ts // before — silently erased, now error // import { User } from './types'; // after import type { User } from './types'; import { fetchUser } from './api'; type Props = { user: User }; export function UserCard({ user }: Props) { return {user.name}; } // mixed import { type Config, createConfig } from './config'; createConfig({} as Config); // only createConfig emitted // re-export export type { Props as CardProps }; export { UserCard }; declare function fetchUser(x: string): Promise; ```

title: How do you choose between `NoInfer<T>`, `satisfies`, and `const` type params when designing APIs?
description: Compare three inference-control tools: `NoInfer<T>` vs `satisfies` vs `<const T>` — which to reach for in config factories and builder patterns.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">infer site</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">fn<T>(x: T)</text><line class="d-edge" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">NoInfer<T></text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">block inference</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Use default T</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">not widened site</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** `<const T>` narrows the inferred type, `NoInfer<T>` blocks a position from influencing inference, and `satisfies` validates without changing the inferred variable's type — they compose but solve different directions.

**Core concept.** Use `<const T>` when you want call-site literals to stay narrow (route arrays, discriminants). Use `NoInfer<T>` when one param should be authoritative and another must only be checked (canonical `initial` vs `fallback`). Use `satisfies` at the **value declaration** side, not the function signature — it checks a value against a wider type while keeping its literal type for later.

How it works — Example: `function define<const T>(x: T, y: NoInfer<T>)` infers narrow `T` from `x` alone, then checks `y` without widening. Contrast `const cfg = { mode: "dark" } satisfies Theme` — here `Theme` is the check, but `typeof cfg.mode` stays `"dark"`. Stacking: `define<const T>(x: T): T` + `const v = define({a:1}) satisfies Record<string, number>` gives both. Common mistake: using `satisfies` inside the function signature — it only works on expressions, not type params.

Rule of thumb: control the callee's `T` with `<const>`/`NoInfer`; control the caller's variable type with `satisfies`.

| Goal | Tool | Example | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Keep literals | `<const T>` | `declare function f<const T>(x:T)` | `string[]` -> `readonly ["a"]` |
| Block second param from widening | `NoInfer<T>` | `f<T>(a:T, b:NoInfer<T>)` | `T` from `a` only |
| Validate value, keep literal | `satisfies` | `const v = {…} satisfies T` | `typeof v` stays narrow |
| All three together | compose | `f<const T>(x:T):T` + `v satisfies T` | narrow + safe |

> **Tip:** Don't wrap every param in `NoInfer` — it hides useful errors; add it only to the non-canonical position, and document which argument is authoritative.

```ts
// narrow + authoritative + validated
declare function define<const T>(primary: T, fallback: NoInfer<T>): T;

const a = define({ mode: 'dark' as const, scale: 1 }, { mode: 'dark', scale: 2 });
// T inferred from first arg only — narrow literal kept

// satisfies side
type Theme = { mode: 'light' | 'dark'; scale: number };
const cfg = { mode: 'dark', scale: 1 } satisfies Theme;
type M = typeof cfg.mode; // "dark" — preserved

// anti-pattern: NoInfer everywhere — no inference at all
// declare function bad<T>(a: NoInfer<T>, b: NoInfer<T>): T; // T becomes unknown
```

title: How do `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` and TS 5.6+ checks harden 2025 codebases?
description: New strictness flags shipping after 5.5: `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `noImplicitOverride`, and 5.6 `noCheck` interactions with `isolatedDeclarations`.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">TS Source</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">types + emit</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="410" y="85" text-anchor="middle">Checker</text><text class="d-sub" x="410" y="105" text-anchor="middle">narrow & infer</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="510" y1="90" x2="590" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="590,90 580,84 580,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="600" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="700" y="85" text-anchor="middle">.d.ts / JS</text><text class="d-sub" x="700" y="105" text-anchor="middle">safe emit</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` makes `arr[0]` be `T | undefined`; `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` distinguishes `prop?: string` from `prop?: string | undefined` — both catch 2024's most common production `undefined` crashes.

**Core concept.** 2025+ best practice is `strict: true` **plus** `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true` and `exactOptionalPropertyTypes: true`. The former forces you to handle `array[index]` and `Record<string,T>[key]` possibly being `undefined`, matching JS truth; the latter prevents assigning `undefined` to an optional prop that wasn't declared as `| undefined`.

How it works — With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `const a=[1,2]; const x=a[5]` is `number | undefined`, so `a[0].toFixed()` errors until you guard. Combined with `isolatedDeclarations`, indexed access types require explicit checks. `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` makes `{x?: string}` no longer accept `{x: undefined}` unless you write `x?: string | undefined` — catching API shape bugs where absence vs explicit `undefined` matters (React props, JSON patch). `noImplicitOverride` and `noUnusedLocals` round out strictness. TS 5.6 adds `noCheck: true` per-file for generated code without skipping emit.

Mitigation: use `arr.at(0)` which is already `T|undefined` typed, `.filter(Boolean)` narrowing (5.5), and `Map` for dictionaries where key absence is explicit.

| Flag | Off | On | Fix pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` | `arr[0] is T` | `T | undefined` | `arr[0] ?? fallback`, `if (x!=null)` |
| `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` | `{x?:string}` allows `undefined` | needs `| undefined` | declare `x?: string | undefined` |
| `noImplicitOverride` | `override` optional | must write `override` | add keyword |
| `noCheck: true` (file) | type errors emit fail | skip check, still emit | for generated files |

> **Tip:** Enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` incrementally with `// @ts-expect-error` audits — it surfaces dozens of real bugs in `Object.keys`, `array[i]`, and `Record` lookups.

```ts
// tsconfig: { "strict": true, "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true, "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true }

const arr = ['a','b'];
const first = arr[0]; // string | undefined — must guard
if (first !== undefined) first.toUpperCase();

type Props = { name?: string };
const p1: Props = {}; // ok
// @ts-expect-error with exactOptionalPropertyTypes
const p2: Props = { name: undefined }; // needs name?: string | undefined

class Base { greet(){} }
class Child extends Base {
  override greet(){} // must use override with noImplicitOverride
}

// generated file
// @ts-nocheck — skip checking but keep emit
export const generated = { x: 1 };
```

title: How do you author library types that pass `isolatedDeclarations` for `oxc` / `tsdown` builds?
description: Checklist for library authors: explicit return types, no `satisfies` leaks, `verbatimModuleSyntax` re-exports, and tools (`publint`, `attw`, `tsdown`).
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">TS file</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">code + types</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="220" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="420" y="85" text-anchor="middle">isolatedDeclarations</text><text class="d-sub" x="420" y="105" text-anchor="middle">emit .d.ts alone</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="530" y1="90" x2="610" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="610,90 600,84 600,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="620" y="40" width="180" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="710" y="85" text-anchor="middle">No checker needed</text><text class="d-sub" x="710" y="105" text-anchor="middle">oxc / swc / esbuild</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** Exported symbols must have explicit types, no expression-computed types, and `type`-only imports under `verbatimModuleSyntax` — then `oxc`/`swc` can emit `.d.ts` per file without the checker.

**Core concept.** `isolatedDeclarations` + `oxc` is 2025's fastest library pipeline (form builds 5–10× faster than `tsc`). To pass, add return types to every exported function, annotate `const` exports (`export const x: T = …`), avoid `as const satisfies Complex<T>` at export boundaries (move `satisfies` inside), and use `verbatimModuleSyntax` style `import type` so declaration emit doesn't need to know if an import is a type.

How it works — `tsdown`/`unplugin-isolated-decl` runs per file: `export function f(x) { return cond ? 1 : "a" }` fails because the conditional union can't be resolved file-locally without analyzing `x`'s call sites — annotate `f(x: string): string|number`. `export * from "./inner"` works only if `inner` itself has `isolatedDeclarations`. Computed property keys and `infer` at top level need explicit aliases. Test with `tsc --isolatedDeclarations --noEmit` and `publint` for export map coherence.

Packaging: emit `dist/*.js` + `dist/*.d.ts` per entry, mirror `exports` conditions, and run `attw --pack` in CI.

| Export | Fails isolatedDeclarations | Passes | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `export const x = get()` | implicit call result | `export const x: string = get()` | needs local type |
| `export function f(x){return x}` | param implicit any | `f(x: string): string` | per-file inf. |
| `export const y = {a:1} as const satisfies T` | computed from T | `export const y: T = {a:1} as const` | no cross-file check |
| `import { Props }` | needs checker to erase | `import type { Props}` | verbatim |

> **Tip:** Add `typescript@5.5+` peer and run `tsc --isolatedDeclarations --declaration --emitDeclarationOnly --noEmit false` locally before switching bundler to `oxc`.

```ts
// lib/src/index.ts — isolatedDeclarations clean
import type { User } from './user';
import { fetchUser } from './fetch';

// explicit types on all exports
export type { User };

export async function getUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
  return fetchUser(id);
}

export const DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE: number = 20;

export function formatUsers(users: readonly User[]): string[] {
  return users.map(u => u.name);
}

// re-export — inner must also be isolatedDeclarations clean
export type { FetchOptions } from './fetch';
declare function fetchUser(id: string): Promise<User>;
```

title: How do you debug type-resolution and ESM/CJS mismatches with `traceResolution` and `explain`?
description: Use `npx tsc --traceResolution`, `--explainFiles`, `arethetypeswrong`, and `publint` to diagnose why types resolve to the wrong file.
answer:
<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><rect class="d-box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="120" y="85" text-anchor="middle">dual pkg</text><text class="d-sub" x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle">CJS + ESM</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="220" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="300,90 290,84 290,96"/><rect class="d-box-accent" x="310" y="40" width="220" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="420" y="85" text-anchor="middle">arethetypeswrong</text><text class="d-sub" x="420" y="105" text-anchor="middle">attw --pack</text><line class="d-edge-accent" x1="530" y1="90" x2="610" y2="90"/><polygon class="d-arrow" points="610,90 600,84 600,96"/><rect class="d-box" x="620" y="40" width="180" height="100" rx="12"/><text class="d-text" x="710" y="85" text-anchor="middle">false ESM?</text><text class="d-sub" x="710" y="105" text-anchor="middle">.js vs .d.ts mismatch</text></svg>

**TL;DR:** `--traceResolution` logs every `moduleResolution` probe, `--explainFiles` shows why a file was included, and `attw` replays consumer resolvers — together they pinpoint ESM/CJS mismatch in minutes.

**Core concept.** When `cannot find module "./x.js"` or `attw` reports `FalseESM`, the cause is usually `moduleResolution`/`exports` mismatch. `tsc --traceResolution --noEmit` prints the search: `Resolving "./foo" from /src/index.ts -> probing ./foo.ts -> ./foo.js -> node_modules` with condition `import`/`require`/`types` applied. `--explainFiles` tells you *why* `dist/index.cjs` was pulled instead of `dist/index.mjs`.

How it works — Add `"traceResolution": true` temporarily or run `npx tsc --traceResolution --noEmit 2>&1 | grep foo`. Look for `Matched 'exports' condition` and extension probing. Pair with `npx @arethetypeswrong/cli --pack --format json | jq` for structured diff of expected vs actual entry. `publint` catches missing `files`/`exports` entries and `package.json` type mismatches. In editors, `TS: Go to definition` on `import` shows the resolved `.d.ts` — if it points to the wrong `dist`, your `types` condition is ordered wrong.

Fix ordering: `types` must be **first** in each `exports` condition object; Node picks first match, TS picks `types` only if present.

| Tool | Shows | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| `tsc --traceResolution` | probe steps + `exports` match | import not found / wrong file |
| `tsc --explainFiles` | why file included | duplicate `.d.ts` or unexpected dep |
| `attw --pack` | consumer view (CJS/ESM/bundler) | publishing check |
| `publint` | `package.json` shape + `exports` | pre-publish |
| `areTheTypesWrong --format json` | diff per entry | CI gating |

> **Tip:** Keep a `scripts/attw: attw --pack` npm script and gate CI on zero `False*` — cheaper than debugging consumer issues post-publish.

```ts
// debug flow
// 1) trace
// npx tsc --traceResolution --noEmit 2>&1 | grep "foo.js"
// -> Resolving "./foo.js" from src/index.ts
// -> Found 'package.json' ... matched exports { ".": { "import": ... } }

// 2) explain why dist file picked
// npx tsc --explainFiles | grep "dist/index.d"
```
